learning_objective: 🎯 Discover your fundamental rights as an Indian citizen, how you can protect them, and the duties the state and citizens owe to the nation!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: These are essential rights guaranteed to all citizens. They include Right to Equality, Freedom, against Exploitation, Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and the Right to Constitutional Remedies.

Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called this the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution. It allows citizens to approach the Supreme Court or High Courts if their fundamental rights are violated, using specific orders called 'Writs'.
Courts can issue writs: Habeas Corpus (produce the body), Mandamus (we command), Prohibition (forbid lower courts), Quo Warranto (by what authority), and Certiorari (to be certified).

Found in Part IV, these are guidelines for the government to create a just and equal society (welfare state). Unlike Fundamental Rights, they are non-justiciable (you can't go to court to enforce them).
While Fundamental Rights protect political democracy and individual freedom, DPSPs aim for social and economic democracy. They are complementary to each other.

fun_activity.title: ⚖️ Be the Judge
fun_activity.instructions: If the police arrest someone without telling them why and keep them locked up for days, which Writ would you use to free them? (Hint: It means 'to have the body'). It's Habeas Corpus!

exam_tips: 📌 Differentiate clearly between Fundamental Rights (justiciable) and Directive Principles (non-justiciable).
📌 Memorize the names and basic meanings of all five Writs.
📌 Remember that Fundamental Rights are not absolute; the government can impose 'reasonable restrictions' during emergencies.
quick_recap: ⭐ The Right to Property was removed from Fundamental Rights and made a legal right in 1978.
⭐ Fundamental Duties (Part IVA) were added later; they remind citizens that rights come with responsibilities.
⭐ Article 21 (Right to Life and Personal Liberty) cannot be suspended even during a National Emergency.
